title: Power Tool Manufacturing
one_liner: US power tool manufacturers sell into construction, industrial, repair and DIY markets, but import penetration and tariff volatility keep pricing and margins under pressure.
overview: This industry manufactures power-driven hand tools, including battery-powered, corded, pneumatic, hydraulic, powder-actuated and internal combustion-driven handheld tools, plus related replacement parts. The 2021 baseline showed a small domestic manufacturing base with $3.8 billion of revenue, $7.9 billion of imports, $889 million of exports and imports supplying 73.2% of US domestic demand. By 2025-2026, demand is split between soft retail and housing-linked DIY conditions and more resilient professional/industrial replacement cycles. Cordless platforms, brushless motors, lithium-ion batteries, connected tools and accessories are the growth center, while commodity corded tools and price-led imported tools remain margin pressure points.

key_stats.market_size: $4.3 billion in estimated 2026 US manufacturing revenue, based on the baseline forecast path to 2026
key_stats.growth: +2.4% 2021-2026 CAGR in the baseline forecast; 2026 demand conditions are mixed because May 2026 total construction spending was $2.210 trillion SAAR, down 1.5% from May 2025
key_stats.profit_margin: 12.6% industry profit margin in 2021 baseline; Stanley Black & Decker Tools & Outdoor reported 10.1% segment profit margin in 2025
key_stats.imports: $7.9 billion of imports in 2021 baseline; imports satisfied 73.2% of domestic demand in 2021 and were forecast to satisfy 72.0% in 2026
key_stats.exports: $889 million of exports in 2021 baseline, forecast to reach about $1.0 billion by 2026
key_stats.employment: 7,505 employees in 2021 baseline, forecast to reach 8,176 by 2026
key_stats.domestic_demand: $10.8 billion in 2021 baseline domestic demand; third-party US power tools market estimates put 2025 demand around $11.4 billion
key_stats.cordless_market: US cordless power tools revenue was estimated at $3.145 billion in 2025 and $3.437 billion in 2026

baseline_2022.market_size: $3.9 billion in estimated 2022 US manufacturing revenue, derived from the 2021 baseline of $3.8 billion and the baseline 2021-2026 forecast CAGR
baseline_2022.growth: +2.4% in 2022, using the baseline forecast CAGR
baseline_2022.context: The baseline expected recovery from 2020-2021 construction disruption, persistent import penetration above 70.0% of domestic demand, and gradual gains from exports and nonresidential construction recovery.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by selling branded and private-label power tools, tool kits, batteries, chargers, accessories, replacement parts and professional-grade systems through home centers, industrial distributors, online retailers, contractors, OEM channels and export markets. Higher-margin economics come from cordless ecosystems, premium professional tools, batteries, accessories, repair/service programs and platform lock-in, while entry-level corded and generic tools compete heavily on price.
cost_structure: The largest cost buckets are purchased components and materials, including motors, batteries, electronic controls, metal parts, plastics and imported subassemblies. Labor, machining, assembly, warranty/service, freight, tariffs, R&D, marketing and retailer/distributor allowances are also material. The 2021 baseline profit margin was 12.6%, while 2025 company data show margin pressure and recovery from pricing, supply-chain savings and tariff mitigation. Battery cells, electronic controls and China-linked sourcing are especially exposed to 2025-2026 tariff and logistics swings.
major_players: Stanley Black & Decker / DeWalt, Craftsman, Stanley, Black+Decker
Emerson Electric / RIDGID-branded professional tools through channel relationships
current_dynamics: Retail power-tool demand softened in 2025 as housing turnover, DIY spending and promotional intensity weakened, while professional construction and industrial replacement demand remained more durable. Stanley Black & Decker reported 2025 Tools & Outdoor sales of $13.158 billion, down 1% from 2024, with organic revenue down 2% but margins improved through pricing and supply-chain actions. TTI reported 2025 sales of $15.3 billion, up 4.4%, with Milwaukee and Ryobi still expanding. In 2026, domestic manufacturers face a demand ceiling from weaker housing starts and lower year-to-date construction spending, but benefit from battery-platform upgrades, professional adoption of cordless tools and tariff-driven incentives to diversify sourcing or nearshore production.
whats_growing: Cordless power tools, lithium-ion battery packs, brushless motors, fast chargers, high-output professional platforms, compact tools, tool tracking/connectivity, accessories, repair parts and jobsite productivity products are growing. The US cordless power tools market was estimated at $3.145 billion in 2025 and $3.437 billion in 2026, with drilling and fastening tools the largest cordless product segment.
whats_shrinking: Commodity corded tools, low-end retail kits, discretionary DIY purchases tied to weak housing turnover, gas/internal-combustion handheld tools where electric alternatives are improving, and China-dependent import programs with limited pricing power are shrinking or losing share. Housing starts were down 8.7% year over year in May 2026, which weighs on new-construction-linked tool demand.
recent_developments: 2025-05-14: The White House modified China reciprocal tariffs, setting an additional 10% duty on PRC-origin articles effective May 14, 2025, adding to tariff complexity for imported tool supply chains.
2026-02-04: Stanley Black & Decker reported 2025 Tools & Outdoor net sales of $13.158 billion, down 1% from 2024, with organic revenue down 2% and segment margin improving to 10.1%.
2026-03-04: Techtronic Industries reported 2025 sales of $15.3 billion, up 4.4%, with Milwaukee up 7.9% and Ryobi up 5.4% in local currency.
2026-06-16: Census reported May 2026 housing starts at a 1.177 million SAAR, down 8.7% from May 2025, signaling weaker new-residential tool demand.
2026-07-01: Census reported May 2026 construction spending at a $2.210 trillion SAAR, down 1.5% from May 2025, with private residential at $930.2 billion and private nonresidential at $738.7 billion.
outlook: The industry should grow slowly through 2026 as domestic production benefits from professional cordless upgrades, infrastructure and industrial demand, and selective reshoring, but the broader US tool market will remain import-heavy. Revenue growth is likely below the high-growth cordless category because many fast-growing batteries, chargers and consumer kits are imported or assembled through global supply chains. Margins should improve for brands with pricing power, proprietary battery ecosystems and supply-chain flexibility, while smaller manufacturers and private-label suppliers remain exposed to tariffs, retailer bargaining power and construction-cycle weakness.
one_sentence: Power Tool Manufacturing is a mature US machinery niche where domestic producers compete on professional-grade cordless platforms, batteries, accessories and brand ecosystems while lower-cost imported tools satisfy most domestic demand.

title: Power Tools & Other General Purpose Machinery Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A mature, trade-exposed machinery segment serving construction, factories, packaging lines, welding shops and maintenance markets.
overview: The industry is broad and cyclical: demand rises when manufacturers invest in equipment, builders buy tools, consumer home-improvement activity is healthy, and export markets are receptive to US-made machinery. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline put industry revenue at $55.6 billion, but current public data for the closest full NAICS proxy, Other General Purpose Machinery Manufacturing (NAICS 3339), show sectoral output of $125.8 billion in 2025, up 6.3% from 2024. Applying that 2022-2025 NAICS output movement to the IBISWorld revenue base implies an estimated 2025 industry revenue near $60.8 billion. Conditions in 2025-2026 are mixed: industrial demand is improving, business equipment output rebounded in mid-2026, but consumer power-tool channels remain soft and tariffs on metals and equipment inputs are keeping cost and pricing discipline central.

key_stats.market_size: 2025 estimated industry revenue of about $60.8 billion, inferred from the 2022 IBISWorld revenue baseline and 2022-2025 growth in BLS/FRED NAICS 3339 sectoral output
key_stats.growth: 2025 growth of 6.3% for NAICS 3339 sectoral output; implied 2022-2025 CAGR of about 3.0% from the same proxy
key_stats.sectoral_output: 2025 NAICS 3339 sectoral output was $125.8 billion, up from $118.4 billion in 2024 and $115.1 billion in 2022
key_stats.employment_context: 2026 machinery manufacturing employment was 1.091 million in July 2026 across NAICS 333, with 35,154 establishments in Q4 2025
key_stats.pricing: 2026 machinery manufacturing producer price index reached 198.238 in June 2026, rising 0.3% month over month
key_stats.profitability: 2022 baseline industry EBIT margin was 4.3%; large branded peers reported much higher 2025 segment margins, such as Stanley Black & Decker Tools & Outdoor adjusted segment margin of 10.7% and ITW Welding operating margin of 33%

baseline_2022.growth: 3.2% revenue growth in 2022 and 0.7% annualized revenue growth over 2017-2022
baseline_2022.exports: $18.9 billion in 2022, equal to 34.0% of revenue
baseline_2022.imports: $43.8 billion in 2022, satisfying 54.4% of domestic demand

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers earn revenue by selling finished equipment, replacement parts, accessories, consumables, custom machinery, integrated production systems and aftermarket service. Major channels include distributors, home-improvement retailers, industrial supply houses, direct sales to manufacturers, construction contractors, automotive and aerospace customers, food and pharmaceutical packagers, and export customers. Higher-value revenue comes from branded cordless tools, automated welding and cutting cells, packaging equipment, engineered fluid-power systems and application-specific machinery where engineering support and uptime matter more than lowest price.
cost_structure: The main costs are purchased materials and components, especially steel, aluminum, motors, electronics, batteries, castings, machined parts, hydraulics, pneumatics and imported subassemblies. Labor is material because many products require machining, fabrication, welding, assembly, testing and engineering support; BLS reported 2026 average hourly earnings of $39.26 for all machinery manufacturing employees in July 2026. Profitability is pressured by metal-price volatility, tariffs, freight, channel rebates, warranty costs and price competition from imports, while automation, SKU simplification, scale purchasing and premium product mix support margins.
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 cycle is stronger on industrial and infrastructure-linked machinery than on consumer power tools. BLS/FRED data show NAICS 3339 output rebounding 6.3% in 2025 after a 3.3% decline in 2024, and the Federal Reserve reported manufacturing output up at a 4.7% annual rate in Q2 2026. Construction demand is uneven: nonresidential, infrastructure, data-center and factory projects are supporting equipment, welding and packaging demand, while housing and retail power-tool demand remain softer. Import exposure remains high, and 2025-2026 tariff changes on steel, aluminum, copper and selected industrial equipment have made pricing, sourcing and North American supply-chain strategy more important.
whats_growing: Industrial automation, robotic welding, cutting systems, packaging machinery for food, beverage and pharmaceuticals, fluid-power and motion-control products tied to factory upgrades, aftermarket service, replacement parts, and higher-margin professional cordless platforms are growing. Infrastructure, aerospace, defense, energy, data-center and reshoring projects are supporting demand for engineered machinery and welding systems in 2025-2026.
whats_shrinking: Consumer and DIY power-tool volumes tied to retail home-improvement channels are weaker, especially in North America in 2025. Lower-end imported tools face margin pressure from tariffs and freight, while mature standard machinery, manual equipment and undifferentiated components are losing share to automation, connected tools and more efficient integrated systems. Some packaging and industrial precision equipment categories softened in 2025 as customers delayed capital spending.
recent_developments: 2025: BLS/FRED NAICS 3339 sectoral output reached $125.8 billion, up 6.3% from 2024.
2025: Stanley Black & Decker Tools & Outdoor sales were $13.158 billion, down from 2024 as North American power-tool retail demand softened.
2025: Lincoln Electric net sales rose to $4.233 billion, with equipment sales of $1.080 billion and automation sales of $870 million.
2025: ITW reported $1.9 billion of Welding revenue with a 33% operating margin and $1.8 billion of Specialty Products revenue with a 31% operating margin.
June 2026: The Federal Reserve reported manufacturing output up at a 4.7% annual rate in Q2 2026 and total industrial production 1.1% above June 2025.
June 2026: US tariff changes on steel, aluminum, copper and selected industrial equipment increased cost and sourcing uncertainty for machinery producers.
outlook: The industry should grow modestly through 2026, with better momentum in industrial, infrastructure, automation, welding and packaging machinery than in consumer power tools. A reasonable 2026 view is low-single-digit revenue growth from the 2025 estimated revenue base, supported by manufacturing output gains and business equipment demand, but constrained by high import penetration, uncertain tariffs, cautious home-improvement retail channels and capital-spending selectivity. Margin improvement will depend on price realization, tariff mitigation, productivity, sourcing flexibility and mix shift toward engineered systems and aftermarket revenue.
one_sentence: US power tools and other general-purpose machinery manufacturers sell a broad mix of powered hand tools, welding equipment, packaging machinery, industrial furnaces, fluid-power products, pumps, motors, scales and specialty machinery into construction, manufacturing, auto repair, food, beverage, pharmaceuticals and export markets.

title: Pre-Made Salsa Production
one_liner: A mature but still flavor-led packaged food niche where salsa producers win through shelf space, Mexican food adoption, snacking occasions and premium authenticity.
overview: Pre-made salsa production sits inside the broader US sauces, dips and spreads market, supplying branded, private-label and foodservice salsa in jars, tubs, pouches and bulk formats. The 2021 baseline described a mature industry supported by Hispanic population growth, mainstream Mexican cuisine, chips-and-dip snacking and the view of salsa as a low-fat, vegetable-forward condiment. Current 2025-2026 data point to a stronger consumer market than the old low-growth baseline implied: the US salsas, dips and spreads market was reported at $1.5 billion in 2024, with salsa holding about 45% share, implying roughly $0.68 billion for salsa in 2024 and about $0.77 billion in 2026 if category growth and share hold. Producers face a split market: national brands such as Pace, Tostitos and Herdez anchor mass retail, while regional, organic, refrigerated and authentic-style products fight for premium shelf space.

key_stats.market_size: 2026 estimated US salsa segment revenue of about $0.77 billion, derived from a $1.5 billion 2024 US salsas/dips/spreads market and salsa's 45% 2024 share, grown at the reported 6.5% CAGR to 2026
key_stats.growth: 2024-2034 reported CAGR of 6.5% for US salsas/dips/spreads; 2026-2033 reported CAGR of 8.7% for broader US Latin sauces
key_stats.category_context: 2024 US salsas/dips/spreads market size was $1.5 billion; salsa was reported as the largest product segment at about 45% share
key_stats.price_pressure: June 2026 BLS CPI showed spices, seasonings, condiments and sauces up 2.8% year over year, while sauces and gravies were up 1.7% year over year
key_stats.input_pressure: June 2026 USDA ERS reported fresh vegetable prices up 9.9% year over year and fresh tomato prices up 19.5% year over year
key_stats.seasonality: Instacart 2025 purchase data showed salsa order share up 96% during Big Game weekend versus the 12-month average

baseline_2022.market_size: About $842 million in 2022 revenue, estimated from the baseline file's $840 million 2021 revenue and 0.28% projected 2021-2027 CAGR
baseline_2022.growth: 0.28% projected annual revenue growth for 2021-2027 in the baseline file
baseline_2022.profit_margin: 1.4% in the baseline file's 2021 key statistics, after pandemic-era cost and demand volatility
baseline_2022.establishments: 159 establishments in 2021 baseline, projected to grow at a 2.65% CAGR from 2021-2027
baseline_2022.employment: 2,616 employees in 2021 baseline, projected to grow at a 1.30% CAGR from 2021-2027

how_it_makes_money: Producers earn revenue by manufacturing salsa under owned brands, licensed brands, co-manufacturing contracts and private-label programs. Branded sales flow through grocery, mass, club, convenience, e-commerce and foodservice distributors, while bulk salsa is sold to restaurants, institutional kitchens and prepared-food manufacturers. Margin comes from scale purchasing of tomatoes, peppers, onions, vinegar, spices, jars, lids and labels; automated filling and thermal processing; slotting and promotion discipline; and premium pricing for refrigerated, organic, fire-roasted, salsa verde, guacamole-style, fruit-forward and authentic regional recipes.

cost_structure.purchases: Largest cost bucket; tomatoes, tomatillos, peppers, onions, vinegar, spices, preservatives, glass or plastic packaging, lids, labels and corrugate typically determine gross margin swings
cost_structure.labor: Modest but important cost; baseline wage cost was about 6.1% of 2019 revenue and 2021 baseline wages were $83 million
cost_structure.packaging_and_freight: Material cost exposure is high because jars, caps, labels, cases, pallets and truckload freight move with energy, glass, resin and distribution markets
cost_structure.marketing_and_trade_spend: Large brands spend heavily on promotions, retailer programs, coupons, display allowances and shopper marketing to protect shelf position
cost_structure.profit: Baseline profit margin was 1.4% in 2021 key statistics; older 2019 text in the file estimated 5.7%, showing margin sensitivity to input and channel conditions

major_players: MegaMex Foods / Herdez / La Victoria / Chi-Chi's
Private-label and regional refrigerated salsa producers
current_dynamics: Demand is being pulled by at-home snacking, Mexican meal kits, tacos, burrito bowls, foodservice menu penetration and consumers using salsa as both a dip and cooking sauce. The strongest growth is in products that feel more authentic, premium or convenient: salsa verde, charred and fire-roasted recipes, refrigerated tubs, squeeze formats, single-serve cups, organic claims and sauces that bridge salsa, marinade and meal preparation. At the same time, mainstream center-store brands face unit pressure from value-seeking consumers, private label and category crowding across queso, guacamole, hummus and hot sauce.
whats_growing: Salsa verde, authentic Mexican brands, fire-roasted and charred profiles, refrigerated fresh salsa, organic and cleaner-label products, smaller convenient packs, Walmart and club-channel value packs, foodservice-ready bulk formats, and cross-use products that can work as salsa, topping, cooking sauce or marinade.
whats_shrinking: Undifferentiated shelf-stable red salsa, overly promotional mainstream jars, slow-moving mild flavors, brands without authentic or value positioning, and premium products that cannot justify higher price points during grocery-budget pressure.
recent_developments: 2024: The US salsas/dips/spreads market was reported at $1.5 billion, with salsa representing about 45% of sales.
Dec 2024: PepsiCo acquired Strauss Group's remaining 50% stake in Sabra, making the refrigerated dips company wholly owned and strengthening PepsiCo's adjacent dips platform.
Feb 2025: PepsiCo reported Frito-Lay North America net revenue down 1% and unit volume down 2.5%, with Tostitos among brands seeing mid-single-digit volume declines.
Jan 2026: Instacart reported 2025 Big Game weekend order share up 96% for salsas versus the 12-month average, underscoring event-driven demand.
Mar 2026: A US Latin sauce market forecast estimated the broader category at $4.694 billion in 2026 with an 8.7% CAGR through 2033.
Apr 2026: Herdez launched an Asada line at Walmart, extending the brand from salsa into marinades, seasonings and Mexican-style BBQ sauces priced under $4.
outlook: The next several years should be healthier than the baseline's low-growth outlook if producers can balance value pricing with flavor innovation. Volume growth will likely remain uneven because center-store food shoppers are price-sensitive and large snack brands have seen unit pressure, but salsa benefits from strong usage breadth: dipping, topping, cooking, entertaining and foodservice. Margin risk is meaningful in 2026 because vegetable and tomato costs are elevated, making pricing, pack architecture and procurement discipline critical. Best-positioned producers will have either scale and retail leverage, authentic Mexican brand equity, refrigerated freshness credentials or private-label manufacturing relationships.
one_sentence: US pre-made salsa producers manufacture refrigerated and shelf-stable tomato-, tomatillo- and chile-based salsas for grocery, club, convenience, foodservice and private-label channels, with growth now coming more from premium flavors, authentic Mexican positioning and meal-solution use than from basic household penetration.

title: Precast Concrete Manufacturing in the US
one_liner: A localized, infrastructure-exposed concrete-products industry supported by public works but pressured by weak private building demand and higher input costs.
overview: Precast Concrete Manufacturing in the US is a mature, fragmented manufacturing industry whose demand follows construction put-in-place, especially utilities, water, highway, bridge, multifamily, industrial and commercial work. The 2022 IBISWorld baseline showed revenue of $15.7 billion and 1.4% growth in 2022, with profit at 6.2% of revenue. A May 2025 IBISWorld-distributed update reported industry revenue had declined at a 0.4% CAGR to $16.3 billion through 2023, including 3.1% growth in 2023. For 2025-2026, public infrastructure, water systems, data centers and institutional work are the main offsets to weaker residential permits, softer nonresidential building spending and elevated cement, concrete-products and financing costs.

key_stats.market_size: 2023: $16.3 billion industry revenue for NAICS 32739 Precast Concrete Manufacturing in the US; 2025: $22.2 billion broader US precast concrete market estimate from IMARC; 2025: approximately $16.8-$17.2 billion implied NAICS-scale revenue range using the 2023 IBISWorld base and low-single-digit construction-linked growth.
key_stats.growth: 2023: +3.1% industry revenue growth; 2020-2025: +1.7% employment CAGR; 2025: +1.5% employment growth; 2026-2034: 5.9% CAGR forecast for the broader US precast concrete market.
key_stats.profitability: 2022: $976 million EBIT profit and 6.2% profit margin in the baseline.
key_stats.construction_spending: May 2026: total US construction spending was $2.210 trillion SAAR, down 1.5% from May 2025; first five months of 2026 were $858.4 billion, down 2.7% from the same 2025 period.
key_stats.public_infrastructure: May 2026: public construction was $541.2 billion SAAR and highway construction was $150.6 billion SAAR.
key_stats.housing: June 2026: housing starts were 1.427 million SAAR, up 3.5% from June 2025, while permits were 1.367 million SAAR, down 2.3% from June 2025.
key_stats.pricing: 2025: BLS precast concrete products PPI averaged 413.240; June 2026: the index was 442.260, about 7.2% above June 2025.

baseline_2022.product_mix: 2022: 63.7% precast concrete products, 17.6% precast building systems and components, 14.6% prestressed concrete products, 4.1% other products.

how_it_makes_money: Manufacturers sell engineered precast and prestressed components to contractors, utilities, developers and public agencies. Revenue comes from casting standardized and custom products in reusable molds, curing them off-site, and delivering them to job sites where speed, quality control, durability and reduced on-site labor justify a premium over cast-in-place work. Key products include manholes, vaults, drainage structures, water-retention systems, slabs, wall panels, beams, bridge girders, railroad ties, roof tiles, posts and poles.
cost_structure: The 2022 baseline had wages of $3.507 billion, equal to about 22.3% of 2022 revenue, and EBIT profit of $976 million, equal to 6.2% of 2022 revenue. The largest operating costs are cement, aggregates, steel reinforcement, admixtures, molds/forms, plant labor, cranes, energy, maintenance, freight and project engineering. Transport distance is a hard economic constraint because finished precast is heavy and low value-to-weight, so plants compete regionally and try to protect margins through scale, batching efficiency, repeat molds, local quarry/cement ties and contract pass-throughs for material inflation.
major_players: CRH / Oldcastle Infrastructure: 2025 CRH total revenue was $37.4 billion; 2025 US revenue was $22.8 billion; Americas Building Solutions, which includes infrastructure products, generated $7.1 billion in 2025 revenue.
Quikrete / Forterra / Rinker / Contech: Quikrete completed the Forterra acquisition in 2022, adding major water, drainage, concrete pipe, structural precast and ductile iron pipe operations.
Jensen Precast: privately held regional US producer focused on utility, stormwater, wastewater, transportation and electrical precast products.
Wells: privately held producer of architectural and structural precast systems for commercial, industrial, institutional and multifamily projects.
Tindall Corporation: privately held structural precast and prestressed concrete manufacturer serving buildings, bridges, utility and industrial markets.
Coreslab Structures: North American precast/prestressed concrete producer serving structural and architectural building markets.
Spancrete: precast and prestressed concrete systems producer known for hollowcore, wall panels and structural building components.
Cementir / Vianini Pipe: Vianini Pipe operates in New Jersey and produces reinforced and prestressed concrete pipe, jack pipe and box culverts.
current_dynamics: The 2025-2026 market is being pulled in two directions. Public-sector infrastructure, water, highway, energy and telecom work remains supportive, helped by federal infrastructure funding and aging municipal systems. At the same time, private construction is mixed: June 2026 housing starts improved year over year, but permits were lower; AIA reported 2025 nonresidential building spending fell 2% to $846 billion and forecast a 0.3% decline in 2026. Cement demand and construction materials inflation remain margin risks, with the American Cement Association forecasting a 2.5% decline in US cement consumption in 2026 and BLS data showing elevated 2026 precast concrete product prices.
whats_growing: Demand is growing for water and wastewater structures, stormwater systems, drainage boxes, utility vaults, data-center and energy infrastructure products, public highway and bridge components, institutional work, resilient infrastructure, and modular/pre-engineered building systems that reduce job-site labor and schedule risk. Broader US precast concrete market forecasts published in 2026 point to high-single-digit nominal growth potential through the early 2030s, though the narrower NAICS manufacturing industry is likely to grow more slowly because it excludes concrete block, pipe and ready-mix categories.
whats_shrinking: Residential-facing roof tiles, ornamental products and some multifamily/building components are exposed to weaker 2026 permits and still-high financing costs. Private office, warehouse and manufacturing building demand is uneven, with AIA's July 2026 forecast calling for manufacturing construction spending to decline 11.6% in 2026 after a 6.7% decline in 2025. Imported low-cost concrete products remain a limited but persistent threat in commodity segments, though transport costs and tariffs constrain penetration.
recent_developments: 2025-05: IBISWorld-distributed update reported 2023 industry revenue of $16.3 billion, down at a 0.4% CAGR through 2023 but up 3.1% in 2023.
2025-05: IBISWorld employment statistics reported 64,846 industry employees in 2025, up 1.5% in 2025.
2026-04-30: American Cement Association Spring Forecast projected US cement consumption would decline 2.5% in 2026.
2026-07-01: Census reported May 2026 total construction spending of $2.210 trillion SAAR, down 1.5% from May 2025, with public construction at $541.2 billion SAAR.
2026-07-17: Census reported June 2026 housing starts of 1.427 million SAAR, up 3.5% from June 2025, while permits were 1.367 million SAAR, down 2.3% from June 2025.
2026-07-21: AIA lowered its 2026 nonresidential building construction forecast to a 0.3% decline and raised its 2027 forecast to 3.0% growth.
outlook: The near-term 2026 outlook is cautious but not distressed. Public infrastructure and utilities should keep plant backlogs healthier than private-building indicators alone would imply, while transportation, water, energy and telecom projects support heavier precast and prestressed products. However, weaker 2026 construction spending, lower permits, falling cement consumption and higher PPI readings limit volume growth and pressure margins. Over 2027, the industry should benefit if rates ease and AIA's forecast 3.0% rebound in nonresidential building spending materializes, but upside will likely be strongest for producers tied to infrastructure, data centers, water systems and complex engineered components rather than commodity architectural or residential products.
themes: Precast modularization and faster job-site schedules
Fragmented regional market with selective consolidation
Data center, energy and telecom infrastructure demand
one_sentence: US precast concrete manufacturers cast slabs, panels, beams, manholes, vaults, poles, roof tiles and other cured concrete components for construction, utilities, transportation, water and energy projects.

title: Precision Agriculture Systems & Services
one_liner: Software, sensors, guidance, autonomy and data services that help farms raise yields, reduce inputs and manage field operations more precisely.
overview: Precision agriculture systems and services include software development, testing, data analytics, consulting, GPS/GNSS guidance, yield monitoring, soil and field mapping, variable-rate controls, drone and remote-sensing tools, and connected equipment platforms used by crop and livestock producers. The industry sells both standalone systems and embedded technology for tractors, sprayers, combines, planters and farm-management platforms. Demand is strongest among large commercial row-crop operations because these farms can spread hardware, software and training costs across more acres, while smaller farms often adopt lower-cost tools, retrofit kits or service-provider models first.

key_stats.market_size: $3.68 billion US precision agriculture market in 2025
key_stats.growth: 6.60% global precision agriculture CAGR forecast for 2026-2034; 6.42% North America CAGR forecast for 2026-2034
key_stats.north_america_market_size: $4.71 billion North America precision agriculture market in 2025
key_stats.adoption: 22% of US farms used precision agriculture practices in 2025, down from 27% in 2023 under USDA NASS reporting
key_stats.connectivity: 85% of US farms had internet access in 2025; 55% used broadband and 74% used cellular data plans
key_stats.large_farm_usage: In 2023, guidance autosteering was used by 70% of large-scale US crop-producing farms and yield monitors, yield maps and soil maps by 68% of large-scale crop-producing farms

baseline_2022.market_size: $3.74 billion in 2022, estimated from the IBISWorld baseline of $3.607 billion in 2021 and its 2021-2026 forecast CAGR of about 3.8%
baseline_2022.growth: 3.8% 2022 implied growth under the IBISWorld 2021-2026 projection
baseline_2022.baseline_source: Local IBISWorld baseline file last updated 2021; 2022 value is a projection-based estimate, not a newly published 2022 observation

how_it_makes_money: Operators make money by selling precision hardware, displays, GPS/GNSS receivers, sensors, controllers and retrofit kits; licensing farm-management and analytics software; charging subscriptions for connectivity, data storage, agronomic recommendations and machine optimization; providing installation, integration and consulting services; and selling per-acre or performance-linked services such as targeted spraying and variable-rate prescriptions. OEM relationships matter because precision systems are often factory-installed into machinery, while retrofit channels expand the addressable market across mixed fleets and older equipment.
cost_structure: The cost base is weighted toward engineering labor, software development, technical support, cloud and data infrastructure, electronics, sensors, processors, GNSS components, dealer installation support, sales and marketing, and R&D. The IBISWorld baseline reported 2021 wages of $1.353 billion and a 2021 profit margin of 14.8%, reflecting a high-skilled, IP-heavy model, but margins are pressured by competition, hardware input costs, dealer support requirements and the need to keep platforms interoperable across equipment brands.
current_dynamics: The market is benefiting from labor scarcity, input-cost pressure, rural connectivity upgrades, AI vision systems, satellite and drone imagery, and farm operators' need to document and optimize field decisions. At the same time, broad equipment replacement has been soft: AEM reported US tractor sales down 14.8% and combine sales down 4.3% in December 2025 versus December 2024, and tractor softness continued into 2026. This pushes vendors toward retrofit kits, software subscriptions and ROI-linked pricing rather than relying only on new-machine sales. USDA's 2025 finding that only 22% of US farms used precision practices also shows that adoption is far from saturated, especially outside large crop farms.
whats_growing: AI-enabled targeted spraying, autonomy kits, retrofit guidance, mixed-fleet control platforms, satellite connectivity, farm data platforms, variable-rate nutrient management, drone and remote-sensing services, precision irrigation, soil analytics and per-acre service pricing are growing as farms seek measurable savings in herbicide, fertilizer, fuel, labor and water.
whats_shrinking: Standalone, closed, single-brand precision systems are losing appeal as farmers demand interoperability. New-equipment-dependent precision sales are pressured by the 2025-2026 ag equipment downturn. Basic GPS guidance and yield-monitoring products are more mature on large row-crop farms, so growth is shifting toward software, autonomy, analytics and retrofit upgrades rather than first-time adoption of basic systems.
recent_developments: 2025-01-06: John Deere revealed second-generation autonomous machines at CES 2025, including an autonomous 9RX tractor for large-scale agriculture.
2025-01-13: John Deere released JDLink Boost satellite connectivity to support precision agriculture in fields with weak cellular coverage.
2025-02-03: John Deere launched Precision Essentials, a lower-upfront-cost retrofit kit for adding precision hardware to legacy and mixed-fleet equipment.
2025-04-28: AGCO expanded its PTx dealer network in North America to support precision agriculture sales and service.
2025-08-01: USDA NASS reported that 22% of US farms used precision agriculture practices in 2025 and 85% had internet access.
2025-11-04: John Deere reported See & Spray was used on more than 5 million acres in the 2025 growing season, reducing non-residual herbicide use by nearly 50% on average.
outlook: The industry outlook is positive but not frictionless. Through 2026, farm-income volatility and soft machinery sales may slow large capital purchases, but precision agriculture remains attractive because it can reduce herbicide, fertilizer, seed, water, fuel and labor costs. Growth should come from retrofit-first distribution, connected machine fleets, AI crop protection, autonomy, precision irrigation and software platforms that turn field data into prescriptions and compliance records. Adoption will remain split: large farms will keep adopting integrated systems fastest, while smaller farms will need lower-cost kits, dealer support, service providers and clearer payback.
themes: AI and computer vision in the field
one_sentence: The US precision agriculture systems and services market is moving from GPS guidance and yield mapping toward connected fleets, AI-assisted spraying, autonomy, retrofit kits and subscription data platforms, but adoption remains uneven by farm size and capital availability.
